How Many Compounds Are in a Bottle of Wine?
How Many Compounds Are in a Bottle of Wine?
A scientific overview of wine’s chemical complexity, sensory relevance, acids, trace compounds, and supporting sources.
How Many Compounds Are in a Bottle of Wine?
How Many Compounds Are in a Bottle of Wine?
A scientific estimate of chemical complexity in a single bottle
The short answer: roughly 800 to 1,000 identified compounds, with strong evidence the true total significantly exceeds this figure.

This is one of the most fascinating questions in food science, and
the answer depends critically on how you define 'compound' and what
detection threshold your instruments can reach. What follows is the best
estimate the scientific literature can currently offer.
Figure 1. Supporting visual from the original document.

But volatile aroma compounds are only part of the story. A complete
accounting of wine's chemistry must also include:

• Polyphenols — Several hundred distinct non-volatile compounds — anthocyanins, tannin oligomers and polymers of varying chain length, flavonols, stilbenes, hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives, and their conjugates and reaction products.
• Organic acids — Twenty or more distinct acid species, from the dominant tartaric and malic to minor succinic, citric, pyruvic, lactic, and gluconic acids.
• Amino acids, peptides & proteins — Fifty or more free amino acids plus a large number of small peptides released by yeast autolysis and grape proteolysis during winemaking.
• Polysaccharides & mannoproteins — A range of high-molecular-weight carbohydrate-protein complexes from grape cell walls and yeast cell walls, each of varying composition.
• Lipids & fatty acids — Thirty or more lipid species including medium-chain fatty acids, glycerophospholipids, and sterols from yeast membranes.
• Mineral ions & inorganics — Twenty or more ionic species — potassium, calcium, magnesium, iron, copper, zinc, sulfate, chloride, phosphate — each with distinct roles in wine chemistry.
• Vitamins & cofactors — B-group vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, pyridoxine, folic acid, pantothenic acid) at trace levels, produced or consumed during fermentation.

When all of these categories are included, the total number of
discrete chemical entities in a single bottle of wine — identifiable by
modern mass spectrometry — is realistically estimated at between 1,000
and 2,000 distinct compounds, with some researchers suggesting the
figure may approach or exceed 2,500 when polymeric tannin species of
different chain lengths are counted individually.

The compound count is inherently a moving target because it depends
entirely on the sensitivity and selectivity of analytical instruments.
This is not a trivial point — it fundamentally changes the answer across
different eras of wine science:
1970s GC-MS analysis: ~200 volatile compounds detectable in a typical wine
Today's Orbitrap & HRMS: Potentially 2,000+ compounds detectable, many still uncharacterized

The same bottle of wine re-analyzed on progressively more sensitive
instruments would yield a higher compound count each time. This means
the question 'how many compounds are in wine?' does not have a fixed
answer — it is a function of the state of analytical chemistry at the
moment of asking.

This is what makes wine uniquely complex as a food matrix. It is an
aqueous ethanol solution that has been biologically transformed by
multiple organisms — the grapevine, Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast,
lactic acid bacteria, and sometimes Botrytis cinerea — over an extended
period ranging from weeks to decades. Each organism produces its own
metabolite spectrum, and these compounds then react with one another
chemically over time, generating further reaction products. Almost no
two bottles are chemically identical, even from the same barrel.

The following table presents a working estimate for a typical red
wine. White wines would show a broadly similar total compound count but
with a different distribution — fewer polyphenols, more terpene and
thiol complexity at the forefront. Aged wines gain compounds through
chemical reactions over time while losing others through hydrolysis and
precipitation.

Of those 1,000+ identified compounds, only a relatively small subset
are considered sensorially active — meaning present above their
individual odor threshold in a typical wine. Ferreira's group at
Zaragoza estimated this number at around 50 to 100 key odorants that
genuinely drive aroma perception in any given wine, with perhaps 20 to
30 dominant in a specific style. The rest contribute at sub-threshold
levels.
Wine contains around 1,000 different aromatic chemicals, but in any given bottle, only about 50–100 of them are present in large enough quantities for your nose to actually detect them.

This does not mean the sub-threshold compounds are irrelevant. There
are at least three mechanisms through which they contribute meaningfully
to wine aroma:

• Synergy — Several compounds present individually below threshold can, in combination, produce a perceptible odor. This is particularly well-documented among ethyl esters, where mixtures at sub-threshold concentrations combine to produce a clear fruity impression.

• Potentiation — Some compounds enhance the perception of others even when themselves below threshold. Beta-damascenone is the best-studied example: at concentrations below its own threshold (~0.05 ppb) it measurably increases the perceived fruitiness of other compounds in the wine matrix.

• Masking & suppression — High concentrations of one compound can suppress perception of another — a phenomenon called 'odor masking'. This means that understanding what a wine smells like requires knowing not just which compounds are present, but how they interact across the full matrix.

These interactions mean that wine aroma cannot be predicted by simply
listing compounds and their concentrations. The interaction space
between 1,000 compounds is, for practical purposes, incalculable. This
is precisely why computational models of wine aroma remain limited and
why trained human sensory evaluation remains irreplaceable in wine
quality assessment.
No two bottles of wine are chemically identical. Even wines from the same barrel, same vintage, and same closure type will diverge over time in bottle due to variation in:

• Dissolved oxygen at bottling — Even small differences in oxygen pick-up during bottling — measurable in parts per million — lead to different rates of oxidative compound formation (acetaldehyde, sotolon, methional) in the finished wine.

• Closure oxygen transmission rate — Natural cork closures vary enormously in oxygen transmission. Two bottles sealed with different corks from the same lot can diverge significantly in aroma profile within 2–3 years of aging.

• Storage temperature and light exposure — Temperature fluctuations accelerate ester hydrolysis and norisoprenoid release. UV light exposure can destroy varietal thiols within hours and accelerate TCA formation in cork-sealed bottles.

• Microbial variation — In wines not sterile-filtered, residual microbial populations differ between bottles. Dormant yeast cells can re-activate under certain conditions, producing additional fermentation metabolites.

• Position in the barrel — Wines drawn from the top vs. the bottom of a barrel during filling differ in polyphenol and mannoprotein content, creating subtle bottle-to-bottle variation before closure is even applied.

A 2010 study by Schneider and colleagues at the University of
Bordeaux estimated that two bottles of the same wine, stored under
identical conditions for ten years, could differ by 15–30% in the
concentrations of key volatile aroma compounds — enough to produce
perceptibly different wines to a trained taster. This natural variation
is part of what makes wine intellectually rich as a subject: the
molecule and the moment of drinking are inseparable.

No single bottle of wine has ever been fully characterized to the
point where every compound has been identified and quantified. Despite
decades of research and enormous advances in analytical chemistry, wine
remains an open problem. Several categories of compounds are
particularly under-characterized:

• High-molecular-weight tannins — The largest condensed tannin polymers (degree of polymerization > 10) are difficult to separate and characterize by conventional MS. Their full structural diversity is unknown.
• Glycoconjugates — Many aroma compounds exist as odorless sugar-bound precursors (glycosides). The full diversity of these bound forms across different grape varieties has not been catalogued.
• Oxidation products — The reaction products of polyphenol oxidation are complex, numerous, and poorly characterized. Many are formed transiently and may not survive sample preparation.
• Microbial metabolites — Wild fermentations involving dozens of yeast and bacterial species produce metabolite profiles that have barely been explored systematically.
• Colloidal species — Wine contains a colloidal phase of protein-tannin-polysaccharide aggregates that do not behave as simple dissolved compounds and whose exact composition is largely unknown.

The advent of non-targeted metabolomics — using high-resolution mass
spectrometry to profile all detectable compounds without prior
assumptions — is beginning to reveal the true scale of wine's chemical
complexity. Early non-targeted studies routinely detect 5,000 to 10,000
distinct mass spectral features in wine, the majority of which remain
unidentified. Assigning chemical identities to these features represents
one of the major current research challenges in enology.

The honest scientific answer, then, is this: in a single bottle of
wine, there are probably between 1,200 and 2,000 discrete compounds
currently identifiable by the best available analytical methods, and a
further several thousand chemical species detectable as mass spectral
signals but not yet assigned structures. Wine remains, in this sense,
one of the most chemically complex objects in everyday human experience
— and one of the least completely understood.

Wine contains roughly 1,000 different chemical compounds that can
evaporate and reach your nose. Of those, only about 50–100 are present
in concentrations high enough to actually be detectable. Among the most
important contributors to a wine’s taste and structure are its organic
acids.

The table below lists the six main acids found in a typical bottle of
wine, their typical concentration ranges, and their role in the wine’s
character.

Dominant acid; unique to grapes. Gives wine firm, crisp structure.
Chemically stable.

Tart, green-apple character. High in cool climates; often converted
to lactic acid via malolactic fermentation.

Soft, buttery acid produced during malolactic fermentation. Common
in reds and Chardonnay.

Byproduct of yeast fermentation with a salty-bitter-sour profile.
Adds mouthfeel complexity.

The acid in vinegar. Normal at low levels; high levels indicate

(regulated in some wine regions).
Note: Concentrations vary significantly by grape variety, climate, and winemaking technique.
Odor threshold: The minimum concentration at which a compound can be detected by smell. Out of ~1,000 volatile compounds in wine, only 50–100 exceed this threshold in any given bottle.
Malolactic fermentation: A secondary fermentation process where sharp malic acid is converted to softer lactic acid, making the wine rounder and less tart.
Total acidity (TA): The sum of all acids in wine, typically expressed in g/L of tartaric acid equivalents. Most table wines fall in the 5–8 g/L range.
A detailed reference for compounds present at sub-ppm concentrations — sulfur traces, aldehydes, nitrogen metabolites, phenolic minors, fatty acids, and Botrytis-specific compounds

The compounds listed here are present in wine at concentrations typically below 1 mg/L (1 ppm), often in the microgram-per-litre (ppb) or even nanogram-per-liter (ppt) range. Despite their minute concentrations, many are sensorially significant — some are detectable at single-digit ppb levels, and a handful shape wine character even at sub-threshold concentrations through synergistic interactions. Concentrations given are typical ranges for commercial wine; individual samples may fall outside these ranges depending on grape health, variety, winemaking technique, and microbial activity.

Sulfur compounds as a class span an enormous range of sensory
character — from the highly desirable (varietal thiols at ppb) to severe
fault compounds detectable at single-digit ppb. The reductive group
below are largely fermentation-derived and form under conditions of low
oxygen, yeast nutrient stress, or prolonged lees contact. Many are
volatile and can dissipate with aeration, but some — particularly the
disulfides and methionol — are persistent and resistant to conventional
remediation.
Origin: Oxidation of methanethiol (two molecules couple), also from microbial S-methionine catabolism

DMDS is one of the most potent reductive sulfur faults in wine. It
forms primarily through the oxidative coupling of methanethiol (CH₃SH)
in the presence of trace oxygen or polyphenol oxidation intermediates.
It is also produced by certain lactic acid bacteria during malolactic
fermentation. Unlike H₂S, DMDS does not respond to copper treatment,
making it particularly problematic. It is found at elevated levels in
wines with poor SO₂ management, those aged in poorly maintained barrels,
or in wines made from sulfur-sprayed vineyards where residual fungicide
sulfur enters the fermentation. DMDS co-occurs commonly with DMS and
methanethiol, and the trio together define what winemakers call
'reduction' in a wine. Some research suggests DMDS is partially
responsible for the 'struck flint' character noted in certain premium
Loire whites and some aged Chardonnay, though this remains debated.
Origin: Oxidative coupling of ethanethiol; reductive fermentation conditions

Diethyl disulfide is the disulfide analogue of ethanethiol, formed by
the coupling of two ethanethiol molecules under mildly oxidative
conditions. It is associated with reductive winemaking — particularly
extended lees contact with insufficient SO₂ protection and minimal
racking. Its onion-garlic character is distinct from but often confused
with DMDS. Treatment options are limited; vigorous aeration or
micro-oxygenation can help but risk oxidative damage to delicate wine
aromas. It is more common in white wines made under heavily reductive
conditions.
Aroma: Cooked potato, cauliflower, boiled vegetables, mild sulfurous
Origin: Yeast Ehrlich pathway catabolism of methionine during fermentation

Methionol is the most abundant sulfur-containing alcohol in wine and
is a normal yeast fermentation product formed from the amino acid
methionine. At concentrations below its sensory threshold (~1 mg/L), it
contributes little detectable character. However, in wines from must
with high methionine content — common in botrytised fruit or over-ripe
grapes — methionol can accumulate to supra-threshold levels. Its
cooked-vegetable character is qualitatively different from the sharp
reductive notes of H₂S and disulfides, and it is far less volatile. It
does not respond to copper treatment. Methionol is also a precursor to
other sulfur compounds through further oxidation and chemical reactions
in the wine matrix.
Aroma: Sweet, rubber, corn, ethereal at trace levels
Origin: Yeast metabolism; also from thermal degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids

Carbon disulfide is a minor but consistently detected sulfur volatile
in wine. It is produced at trace levels by Saccharomyces cerevisiae
during fermentation, particularly in nitrogen-limited conditions. Its
sweet, corn-like character at very low concentrations is generally below
threshold and not considered a fault. At elevated levels (uncommon in
commercial winemaking) it can contribute a rubbery or ethereal quality.
It is worth noting in context because it frequently appears in GC-MS
wine profiles and can interfere with quantification of other sulfur
compounds if analytical methods are not optimized.
Aroma: Odourless to very faint sulfurous at trace levels
Origin: Yeast metabolism; photochemical reactions; thermal decomposition of cysteine

Carbonyl sulfide is among the simplest sulfur compounds detected in
wine and is present in essentially all wines at sub-ppb levels. It is
produced as a minor by-product of yeast fermentation and from thermal or
photochemical decomposition of cysteine and other sulfur-containing
amino acids. At the concentrations found in wine it is entirely below
threshold and has no direct sensory impact. However, it is relevant
analytically because it can be mistaken for other compounds in
sulfur-specific GC detection and because it slowly hydrolyses to H₂S and
CO₂ in aqueous solution, potentially contributing marginally to
reductive character over time.

Beyond acetaldehyde (covered in the main compound tables), wine
contains a range of minor aldehydes formed from lipid oxidation, amino
acid catabolism, and Strecker degradation reactions. These compounds are
particularly relevant in aged and oxidatively handled wines, and several
are formed at the interface of oxygen exposure and polyphenol chemistry.
They are generally present at ppb levels but can be significant
contributors to aroma due to very low perception thresholds.
Aroma: Cut grass, green, fatty, tallow, fresh-crushed leaf
Origin: Lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway acting on linoleic acid in grape cells during crushing

Hexanal is the primary C6 aldehyde formed when grape cells are
ruptured during harvest and crushing. The lipoxygenase enzyme system in
grape skin and pulp rapidly oxidises linoleic and linolenic acids to
form hexanal and related C6 compounds within minutes of crushing.
Hexanal concentrations are therefore highest in freshly pressed must and
decrease significantly during fermentation as yeast reduce aldehydes to
alcohols (hexanal → 1-hexanol). It is most relevant in white winemaking
where skin contact or prolonged pressing can allow LOX activity to build
up green/grassy character. In red wines, the same compounds form but are
largely masked by other phenolic and fermentation-derived aromas. Very
low concentrations post-fermentation can add a fresh, green nuance to
aromatic whites.
Origin: LOX pathway from linolenic acid; also from hydroperoxide lyase action

Trans-2-hexenal is the alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde partner to
hexanal in the C6 lipoxygenase cascade. It is formed from linolenic acid
(rather than linoleic acid) and carries a more intensely green, leafy
character. Like hexanal, it is most abundant in freshly crushed must and
is rapidly reduced by yeast to trans-2-hexenol during fermentation. Its
presence at supra-threshold levels in finished wine generally indicates
either very high enzyme activity during processing, incomplete
fermentation, or poor temperature management during crush. It is
considered a fault at high levels but contributes freshness at trace
concentrations in some styles. Interestingly, its concentration is
significantly affected by grape berry temperature at harvest — cooler
night-harvested grapes often show higher C6 aldehyde levels.
Aroma: Bitter almond, marzipan, cherry stone, almond blossom
Threshold: ~2000 ppb (generally below sensory threshold in wine)
Origin: Yeast catabolism of phenylalanine via the Ehrlich pathway; also from phenylpyruvate decarboxylation

Benzaldehyde is produced as a minor Ehrlich pathway metabolite from
phenylalanine by Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It shares the same metabolic
route as 2-phenylethanol but is an intermediate compound that is
partially reduced to 2-phenylethanol and partially persists in the wine.
Its bitter almond and marzipan character is well-known and at wine
concentrations (generally 10–500 ppb) it sits well below its sensory
threshold (~2 mg/L), meaning it typically does not contribute directly
to aroma perception. However, it can play a role in certain fortified
and sweet wines at higher concentrations, and it is an interesting
marker of phenylalanine nitrogen utilisation by yeast. Benzaldehyde also
occurs in wines made from grapes affected by cherry stem or grape seed
contamination during pressing.
Aroma: Boiled potato, soup, baked potato skin, cooked vegetable
Origin: Strecker degradation of methionine; oxidation of methionol

Methional is one of the most potent aldehyde aroma compounds in wine,
with a perception threshold around 0.5 ppb in a wine matrix. It is
formed primarily through the Strecker degradation reaction — a chemical
reaction between alpha-dicarbonyl compounds (formed during oxidation)
and the amino acid methionine. This means methional formation is
directly linked to wine oxidation events: oxygen ingress through closure
or during handling promotes alpha-dicarbonyl formation which then reacts
with methionine to produce methional. It is a key marker of premature
oxidation in white wines — the phenomenon sometimes called 'premox' in
Burgundy and other aged white wines. It co-occurs with
phenylacetaldehyde and glyoxal during oxidative aging. At sub-threshold
concentrations it may contribute a savoury, umami-like complexity to
aged wines.
Origin: Strecker degradation of phenylalanine; Botrytis cinerea metabolism; yeast Ehrlich pathway

Phenylacetaldehyde is a compound of particular interest because it is
formed through multiple routes and contributes to the aroma of several
distinct wine styles. In botrytised wines (Sauternes, Tokaji,
Trockenbeerenauslese), it is produced directly by Botrytis cinerea
acting on phenylalanine, and is considered a key marker of noble rot
character alongside sotolon and furaneol. In all wines, it can form via
the Strecker degradation of phenylalanine during oxidative aging —
making it another oxidation marker like methional. At very low
concentrations its honey-rose character is often perceived as positive;
at higher levels it can become overripe and cloying. Its threshold of
approximately 1 ppb means wine concentrations are frequently at or above
the sensory threshold, making it a genuine contributor to aroma even at
trace levels.

Yeast and bacteria metabolise nitrogenous compounds from grape must —
amino acids, ammonium, peptides — producing a range of trace
nitrogen-containing compounds as by-products. Several of these are
toxicologically or sensorially significant despite their minute
concentrations.
Threshold: No sensory threshold — not a flavour compound
Origin: Chemical reaction between urea (from arginine catabolism by yeast) and ethanol

Ethyl carbamate is not an aroma compound but is included here for its
toxicological significance. It is classified as a probable human
carcinogen (Group 2A, IARC) and is regulated in several wine-producing
countries, with the EU guideline set at 30 ppb. It forms spontaneously
when urea — a by-product of arginine catabolism by Saccharomyces
cerevisiae during fermentation — reacts with ethanol. Formation is
accelerated by heat and light exposure, making storage conditions
relevant. Wines with high arginine content in the must (common in some
varieties and over-fertilised vineyards) are at higher risk. The enzyme
urease can be used to degrade urea before it reacts with ethanol.
Fortified wines and some late-harvest wines tend to have higher ethyl
carbamate levels due to higher ethanol concentration and the specific
chemistry of their production.
Aroma: Faecal, mothballs at high concentrations; jasmine, floral at very low concentrations
Threshold: ~140 ppb in wine (generally sub-threshold in normal wines)
Origin: Yeast catabolism of tryptophan; some lactic acid bacteria strains

Indole is a bicyclic nitrogen compound with a fascinating dual
character: at very high concentrations its odour is distinctly faecal
and unpleasant, but at extremely low, sub-threshold concentrations it
contributes a sweet, floral, jasmine-like nuance. This dual character is
well-known in perfumery and also applies to wine. In normal commercial
wines, indole concentrations rarely approach the sensory threshold and
it remains a trace background compound. However, in wines made from
over-ripe grapes or grapes with high tryptophan content, and
particularly in wines with sluggish fermentations or certain LAB
activity, indole can accumulate to detectable levels. It has been
associated with the 'barnyard' complex of aromas that also includes
Brettanomyces compounds, though it is produced by different
organisms.
Origin: Microbial catabolism of tryptophan; certain yeasts and lactic acid bacteria

Skatole is the methyl-substituted analogue of indole, with a more
intensely faecal and barnyard character. It is produced by microbial
degradation of tryptophan and has been identified as a contributor to
the complex 'barnyard' aroma in some wines, where it occurs alongside
Brettanomyces-derived 4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol. However,
skatole can be produced by yeast and LAB in the absence of
Brettanomyces, meaning barnyard character is not exclusively a Brett
fault. Like indole, its dual character (pleasant/floral at extreme
dilution, faecal at higher concentrations) is well established. Its
threshold in wine (~40 ppb) is generally above typical wine
concentrations, but it may contribute sub-threshold synergistic effects
alongside other barnyard compounds.
Mousy taint compounds — ACPY, ATHP, ETPY — N-heterocycles — 1–200 ppb
Aroma: Mouse cage, stale popcorn, rice crackers, peanuts (only detectable after saliva raises mouth pH)
Threshold: ~1–5 ppb in alkaline conditions (post-saliva) — uniquely pH-dependent detection
Origin: Oenococcus oeni, Lactobacillus, and Dekkera/Brettanomyces metabolising amino acids (lysine, ornithine) + acetaldehyde at high pH

The mousy taint compounds — 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (ACPY),
2-acetyltetrahydropyridine (ATHP), and 2-ethyltetrahydropyridine (ETPY)
— represent one of the most unusual sensory phenomena in wine. They are
uniquely pH-dependent: in the acidic environment of wine (pH 3.2–3.6)
they exist in their protonated, non-volatile forms and are essentially
imperceptible. Only when wine contacts the alkaline environment of
saliva (pH ~7) do they convert to their free-base, volatile forms and
vaporise retronasally. This means a wine can fail catastrophically on
the palate yet appear clean on the nose — a fact that confounds many
tasting panels. ATHP is generally considered the most potent of the
three. Formation requires the condensation of an amino acid (lysine or
ornithine) with acetaldehyde under conditions of elevated pH, high
temperature, or both. Mousy taint has historically been associated with
spontaneous fermentation and natural/low-sulfite winemaking, as SO₂
suppresses the responsible microorganisms. It is currently an area of
significant research interest given the growth of the natural wine
movement.

Beyond the major polyphenol classes (anthocyanins, condensed tannins,
hydroxycinnamic acids) covered in the main tables, wine contains a range
of minor phenolic compounds at trace levels. Several are formed by
microbial transformation of grape-derived phenolic precursors and have
significant sensory or chemical consequences at low concentrations.
Aroma: Medicinal, antiseptic, clove, pharmaceutical (vinyl phenol); smoky, clove, spice (vinyl guaiacol)
Threshold: Vinyl phenol ~10 ppb; vinyl guaiacol ~40 ppb
Origin: Decarboxylation of p-coumaric acid (vinyl phenol) and ferulic acid (vinyl guaiacol) by yeast PAD1 enzyme

Vinyl phenol and vinyl guaiacol are the immediate precursors to the
Brettanomyces ethylphenol faults (4-EP and 4-EG). They are formed by the
action of a phenolic acid decarboxylase (PAD1) enzyme on p-coumaric acid
and ferulic acid respectively — an enzyme present in both Saccharomyces
cerevisiae (to a limited extent) and very actively in Brettanomyces. In
Saccharomyces-only fermentations, vinyl phenol and vinyl guaiacol can
accumulate at low levels, particularly in white wines fermented with
certain commercial yeast strains selected for high PAD1 activity. In
these cases they are not further reduced to ethylphenols (which requires
an additional vinyl phenol reductase step absent in Saccharomyces) and
may persist in the finished wine. At moderate concentrations their
medicinal, pharmaceutical character is considered a fault in most white
wines, though small amounts of vinyl guaiacol contribute positively to
some styles.
Origin: Brettanomyces decarboxylation of p-cresol precursors; also from tyrosine catabolism

Para-cresol (4-methylphenol) is a Brettanomyces metabolite that is
less commonly discussed than 4-ethylphenol but contributes meaningfully
to the overall 'Brett character' spectrum in affected wines. Its
horse-stable and animal character is distinct from the leather-band-aid
notes of 4-EP, adding a more intensely animal and tarry quality. It is
formed by Brettanomyces from the decarboxylation of
p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate or from tyrosine-based precursors. In wines with
significant Brett activity, para-cresol is often found alongside 4-EP,
4-EG, isovaleric acid, and other Brett metabolites. Its threshold (~55
ppb) means it is frequently sensorially active in Brett-affected wines
even when present at relatively low concentrations.
Origin: Hydrolysis of gallotannins from grape skins and seeds; also released from ellagitannins during oak aging

Gallic acid is a simple phenolic acid that forms as a hydrolysis
product of both grape-derived gallotannins and oak ellagitannins. It is
found in all red wines and in whites aged in oak, though concentrations
vary widely with grape variety, skin contact time, and oak aging regime.
As a taste compound rather than an aroma compound, gallic acid
contributes directly to the bitter and astringent quality of wine. It is
also biologically interesting as a potent antioxidant and as a precursor
to pyrogallol (through decarboxylation by bacteria) which has its own
sensory properties. Gallic acid also reacts with iron to form
iron-gallate complexes that contribute to the blue-black colour of iron
casse (a clarity fault in wines with high iron and tannin content).
Origin: Hydrolysis of oak ellagitannins (vescalagin, castalagin) during barrel aging

Ellagic acid is the hydrolysis product of oak ellagitannins and
accumulates progressively in wine during barrel aging. It has no direct
aroma contribution but plays important structural roles: it can form
insoluble complexes with anthocyanins, contributing to the reddish-brown
precipitate sometimes observed in old wines, and it reacts with wine
polyphenols through oxidative coupling. Its concentration increases with
new oak usage and decreases as barrels are reused. From a health
perspective it has attracted interest as an antioxidant and potential
anti-carcinogenic compound, though concentrations in wine are far below
therapeutic levels. Ellagic acid is also used analytically as a marker
of oak exposure in wines, since it is not present in grape-derived
tannins.

Medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) are produced by yeast during
alcoholic fermentation as intermediates in the fatty acid synthesis
pathway. They are released into the wine when synthesis is interrupted,
typically due to ethanol toxicity or nutrient limitations. At low
concentrations they contribute subtle complexity; at elevated levels
they become unpleasant faults with rancid, soapy, or goat-like
character.
Aroma: Waxy, goat, rancid fat, mildly sour, cheese-like
Origin: Yeast fatty acid synthesis pathway; released as C6 intermediate during fermentation

Hexanoic acid is a C6 medium-chain fatty acid and the shortest of the
three main MCFA faults. It is formed when Saccharomyces cerevisiae
releases C6 intermediates from the fatty acid synthase complex during
fermentation — a process that is exacerbated by high ethanol
concentration, low temperature, and nitrogen deficiency. At trace levels
below its threshold, hexanoic acid is not perceptible but its ethyl
ester (ethyl hexanoate) contributes pleasant apple and anise aromas to
young wine. At higher concentrations the free acid itself contributes a
goat-like, rancid quality that is considered a fault. The threshold
(~420 ppb) is readily reached in fermentations with poor yeast
nutrition, making nitrogen supplementation (DAP or complex yeast
nutrients) an important preventive measure. Hexanoic acid is also found
at elevated levels in wines made from botrytised grapes, as Botrytis
produces it as a secondary metabolite.
Origin: Yeast C8 MCFA synthesis intermediate; also inhibits yeast at elevated concentrations

Octanoic acid is the C8 homologue of hexanoic acid and arguably more
significant because at elevated concentrations it directly inhibits
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, contributing to stuck fermentations. Its
rancid, soapy, goat-like character is a well-known fault and its ethyl
ester (ethyl octanoate) is a pleasant floral-fruity compound found in
young wines. The balance between free octanoic acid (fault) and ethyl
octanoate (positive) is thus directly related to fermentation health and
esterification kinetics. High octanoic acid in must can be remediated by
adding yeast hulls (cell wall preparations) that adsorb the free fatty
acids, or by ensuring adequate yeast nutrition to minimise MCFA release.
Octanoic acid is more prevalent in fermentations from botrytised fruit,
where Botrytis itself produces it as a metabolite.
Origin: Yeast C10 MCFA synthesis intermediate; fermentation stress product

Decanoic acid is the C10 fatty acid homologue, the longest of the
three main MCFA faults in wine. Like hexanoic and octanoic acids, it is
a by-product of interrupted fatty acid synthesis by yeast and is more
prevalent in stressed fermentations. Its rancid-fatty-goat character is
distinct and unpleasant at supra-threshold levels. Unlike the shorter
MCFAs, decanoic acid is less soluble in the water-ethanol wine matrix
and its sensory impact is somewhat self-limiting at higher
concentrations where it may precipitate. Its ethyl ester, ethyl
decanoate, contributes pleasant floral-grape character at low levels in
young wine. The progressive C6-C8-C10 series of MCFAs often occurs
together and their combined sensory impact is additive, meaning even
sub-threshold concentrations of each can produce supra-threshold
combined perception.
Threshold: ~0.23 ppm in wine — relatively low threshold
Origin: Lactic acid bacteria (Oenococcus oeni, Lactobacillus) catabolism of valine; also minor yeast product

Isobutyric acid is a branched-chain fatty acid produced primarily by
lactic acid bacteria through the catabolism of the amino acid valine via
the Ehrlich degradation pathway. It is found in wine at low
concentrations following malolactic fermentation, and elevated levels
are associated with poorly managed MLF — particularly high-temperature
MLF, extended bacterial activity post-diacid conversion, or
contamination with heterofermentative Lactobacillus strains. Its
rancid-butter character is distinct from diacetyl's cream/butter note
and is generally considered a fault. Its relatively low threshold (~230
ppb) means it can be sensorially relevant at concentrations commonly
found in wines with bacterial activity issues. It co-occurs frequently
with isovaleric acid (also a LAB product) in wines with 'cheesy' or
'sweaty' characters.

Botrytis cinerea, the grey rot / noble rot fungus, profoundly
transforms grape chemistry when it infects berries. Under the right
conditions of alternating humidity and dry weather (noble rot), it
concentrates sugars through dehydration while producing a distinctive
array of metabolites. These compounds define the unique aromatic
complexity of Sauternes, Tokaji, Trockenbeerenauslese, and similar
botrytised wines. Many are not found at significant levels in wines made
from healthy grapes.
Threshold: Not well established in wine matrix
Origin: Secondary metabolite of Botrytis cinerea; terpenoid biosynthesis in the fungus

Botrydial is a sesquiterpene-based secondary metabolite produced
exclusively by Botrytis cinerea during grape infection. It is the most
studied of several Botrytis-specific terpenoids and is found in both
grey rot (undesirable) and noble rot (desirable) affected grapes. Its
direct sensory contribution to wine is not fully characterised due to
analytical difficulties and its low concentrations, but it is considered
a marker of Botrytis activity. It is primarily of interest as a
phytotoxin — it contributes to tissue degradation in the grape berry,
facilitating water loss and sugar concentration. At the trace levels
found in finished wine it is below sensory threshold and unlikely to
directly affect aroma. Research into botrydial and related compounds
(dihydrobotrydial, botcinolide) is ongoing.
Origin: Produced by Botrytis cinerea directly as an osmotic stress response; also higher from yeast in high-sugar must

Glycerol production is significantly elevated in botrytised wines for
two reasons: Botrytis cinerea itself produces glycerol as an osmolyte to
survive the high-sugar, low-water-activity environment of infected
berries, and the resulting high-sugar must causes yeast to produce more
glycerol during fermentation as a means of managing osmotic stress.
Glycerol concentrations of 10–20 g/L are typical in Sauternes and TBA
wines, compared to 5–15 g/L in dry wines made from healthy grapes. This
elevated glycerol directly contributes to the characteristic viscous,
unctuous mouthfeel of botrytised sweet wines — the quality sometimes
described as 'liquorous' or 'oily'. It also provides a faint background
sweetness that augments the residual sugar perception.
Threshold: No aroma threshold; taste threshold ~1 g/L
Origin: Direct oxidation of glucose by Botrytis cinerea laccase enzyme

Gluconic acid is produced when Botrytis cinerea's laccase enzyme
oxidises glucose directly in the infected grape berry. It serves as one
of the most reliable chemical markers of Botrytis infection in must and
wine. Healthy grape must typically contains less than 200 mg/L gluconic
acid; must from severely botrytised grapes may contain 2–5 g/L. This is
analytically important because gluconic acid is a strong SO₂ binding
agent, meaning heavily botrytised must requires significantly more total
SO₂ to achieve adequate free SO₂ for microbial protection. Winemakers
measure gluconic acid in botrytised must to adjust SO₂ additions
accordingly. At the high concentrations found in noble rot wines,
gluconic acid contributes marginally to overall acidity and interacts
with wine polyphenols, but its primary significance is as a diagnostic
marker and SO₂ management consideration.
Origin: Botrytis cinerea produces 2-phenylethanol directly from phenylalanine, supplementing yeast-derived levels

While 2-phenylethanol is a normal yeast fermentation product (covered
in the main compound tables), it deserves separate mention in the
context of Botrytis because the fungus itself produces elevated
quantities directly from phenylalanine as part of its secondary
metabolism. In botrytised wines, 2-phenylethanol concentrations can
reach 150–200 mg/L — well above its sensory threshold — contributing to
the distinctive rose-water, floral honey character that is a hallmark of
noble rot wines. This Botrytis-derived increment adds to what yeast
produces during fermentation of the same must, meaning total
2-phenylethanol can be two to three times higher in botrytised wines
than in wines from healthy grapes. It is considered a positive
contributor to the complexity of Sauternes-style wines.

Wine contains a range of inorganic compounds and metal ions at trace
levels. These do not contribute to aroma in the traditional sense but
have significant effects on wine chemistry, stability, clarity, and —
increasingly in the research literature — possible contributions to
mouthfeel and perceived 'minerality'.
Aroma: Metallic, inky at high concentrations (taste/mouthfeel rather than aroma)
Origin: Soil uptake by vine; equipment contamination; fining agents; bentonite

Iron is the most analytically important metal in wine. It exists in
two oxidation states — ferrous (Fe²⁺) and ferric (Fe³⁺) — and
transitions between them drive critical oxidation-reduction reactions in
wine. Ferrous iron catalyses the Fenton reaction, converting hydrogen
peroxide to the highly reactive hydroxyl radical, which causes rapid and
indiscriminate oxidation of wine components. This makes iron content a
key variable in wine oxidative stability. The major practical
consequence of high iron (>5–10 ppm) is iron casse: the formation of
insoluble iron-phosphate (white casse) or iron-tannate (blue
casse) precipitates that cause clarity
problems. Iron fining with potassium ferrocyanide (blue fining,
restricted to EU) or treatment with phytic acid can reduce iron to
acceptable levels. Modern stainless steel winemaking equipment has
significantly reduced iron contamination compared to historical
practices.
Threshold: ~5 ppm metallic taste threshold; EU legal limit 1 ppm in finished wine
Origin: Vineyard copper-based fungicide residues (Bordeaux mixture); copper equipment; deliberate addition for H₂S removal

Copper in wine serves a dual role: at very low levels it is
beneficial (binding and precipitating H₂S and other volatile sulfur
faults), but at elevated levels it causes copper casse (a reddish-brown
haze from copper-protein complexes) and imparts metallic taste. Copper
additions are deliberately used by winemakers to treat H₂S and related
reductive faults — typically 0.1–0.5 mg/L is added and excess copper
later fines out. The EU sets a legal limit of 1 mg/L copper in finished
wine, reflecting concern about both sensory quality and health. Vineyard
applications of Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate + lime) leave copper
residues on grapes that can carry through into must and wine, making
vineyard copper management increasingly important as limits tighten.
Some research has also suggested copper interacts with varietal thiols,
potentially reducing levels of 3MH and 4MMP.
Aroma: None directly; contributes mildly saline/mineral taste at high concentrations
Threshold: Taste: ~400 ppm; contributes to overall ionic mouthfeel
Origin: Yeast oxidation of SO₂ additions; soil sulfate uptake; vineyard sulfur spray residues

Sulfate is a normal and abundant inorganic anion in wine, present at
100–1000 mg/L. It is formed by yeast during fermentation through partial
oxidation of added SO₂ (sulfite), from soil sulfate absorbed by the
vine, and from residual vineyard sulfur (elemental sulfur used as
fungicide) that passes through fermentation. Sulfate itself is
non-volatile and non-aromatic but contributes to overall ionic
composition and mouthfeel. At higher concentrations (above ~400–600
mg/L) it can be perceived as mildly saline or mineral on the palate.
Sulfate has been proposed as one possible contributor to the 'mineral'
sensation in wine — alongside tartaric acid, CO₂, and compounds from
chalky or limestone soils — though the science of wine minerality
remains contested. EU regulations set a maximum of 1 g/L sulfate in wine
(2 g/L if the label states 'sulphureux').
Origin: Soil uptake; galvanised equipment; some fungicide residues

Zinc is a trace metal in wine that is largely unremarkable at typical
concentrations but becomes relevant in certain winemaking contexts. It
is an essential micronutrient for yeast and is sometimes added to yeast
rehydration media to improve fermentation performance. At wine
concentrations (typically 0.1–5 ppm) it contributes no detectable aroma
or taste. However, at elevated levels (uncommon but possible with old
galvanised equipment or certain soil types) it can impart a metallic
note and cause clarity problems through zinc-protein precipitation. Zinc
is measured in routine wine elemental analysis and serves as one
indicator of equipment contamination or unusual terroir chemistry.

Odour thresholds listed throughout this document are measured in model wine solutions and represent the minimum concentration at which a trained assessor can detect the compound in isolation. In real wine, these thresholds shift considerably due to matrix effects: the presence of ethanol, other aromatic compounds, pH, temperature, and dissolved CO₂ all modulate volatile release and receptor binding. Furthermore, many compounds interact synergistically or antagonistically — a well-documented phenomenon in wine flavour science. Beta-damascenone, for example, enhances the perceived fruitiness of other compounds at concentrations well below its own threshold. Conversely, high concentrations of one compound can mask or suppress the perception of another. These interactions mean that the presence of a compound at sub-threshold levels does not imply it has no impact on wine aroma — a key principle when interpreting trace compound data.
